summary.title: Disasters I've seen in a microservices world
summary.one_liner: A practitioner's catalogue of six common microservices failure modes, including over-split services, fragile development environments, end-to-end testing gaps, shared databases, API gateway misuse, and poorly configured timeouts and retries.
takeaways: Splitting a monolith into many small services adds maintenance, deployment coupling and IDE friction costs that are easy to underestimate.
Development environments and end-to-end tests become much harder across many services, and passing tests only show a system worked at one point in time.
A shared database eases migration but creates a single point of failure and hides service dependencies.
API gateways can turn into single points of failure and accumulate business logic if not kept thin and stateless.
Longer timeouts combined with retries without backoff and jitter can worsen outages; treat failure cases as normal, not edge cases.
summary.summary: The author, drawing on years of working on service-oriented systems, describes six recurring problems teams hit after adopting microservices around the 2010s. Each section ("disaster") covers a concrete failure pattern: services that are too small, unmanageable development environments, end-to-end tests that cannot prove a system works, a huge shared database, API gateways that grow into bottlenecks, and timeout/retry configurations that amplify failures. The piece is anecdotal and opinionated rather than tutorial-style, with no code, and it concludes that microservices remain useful for organizational problems if failure handling is designed in from the start.
